title: Quba, the first mosque
hook: on arrival he helps build the first mosque with his own hands (9:108)

segments.voice: Yesterday, As-Sabur, the Patient, the last name on the list. Your line was he waits for you.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is on the road. After years of mockery and pressure in Mecca, he's slipped out of the city by night with Abu Bakr, hidden in a cave, and crossed the desert. The people of Medina have been walking out every morning to the edge of the lava fields to watch for him, going home when the heat gets too much. Then one day a man on a rooftop sees figures in white shimmering on the road, and shouts. He's here. But before he enters the city itself, he stops at a village of palm groves on its southern edge, and stays some days. And one of the first things he does there is build. Today: Quba.
screen: `OUT OF MECCA BY NIGHT.` → `MEDINA WATCHING THE ROAD.` → `A VILLAGE ON THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: Quba was a village of date farms a short way south of the heart of Medina. The Prophet stayed with a local family, and in those days the first mosque of the new community went up, remembered as the first mosque built in Islam. It wasn't grand: a plot of ground marked out, low walls, a place to face the direction of prayer together. Reports gathered by later scholars say the Prophet carried stones for it himself, with his companions, not standing to one side while others worked. The Qur'an speaks of a mosque founded on reverence for God from its very first day, and says it is more fitting to stand in to pray, with people in it who love to purify themselves. Commentators differ over which mosque the verse means. Many say Quba. A hadith in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet pointing to his own mosque in Medina. Some scholars say it praises both. Either way, what it praises is the foundation, not the building: reverence, from the first day. And Quba stayed close to him. Sahih al-Bukhari says he used to go to Quba every Saturday, walking or riding, and pray two units of prayer there. Another hadith, in at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, says a prayer in the mosque of Quba carries the reward of an 'umrah, the lesser pilgrimage. The new life began there: not with a speech, but with a man lifting stones next to everyone else.
screen: `A VILLAGE OF DATE FARMS.` · `HE CARRIED STONES HIMSELF.` · `FOUNDED ON REVERENCE.` · `EVERY SATURDAY TO QUBA.` · then, large: `LIFT A STONE TOO.`

segments.voice: Think of a space you share with other people, a kitchen, a stairwell, a prayer room, a group chat that's gotten messy, and one small thing in it that nobody's handling. Picture yourself doing it, with your own hands, without waiting to be asked, and sit with the reports that the first mosque went up this way.
Quba. The village at the edge of Medina where the Prophet stopped first, and where the first mosque went up. Today's word.
Your line: lift a stone too. The reports say the first mosque rose with his hands among theirs. That's day two hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Pilgrims to Medina visit the Quba mosque, many making wudu at home first and praying two units there, as the Prophet did on Saturdays; the mosque has since been rebuilt and enlarged.

notes: The Prophet carrying stones at Quba: reported in later sources (e.g. at-Tabarani, cited by Ibn Hajar); the stronger reports of carrying bricks concern the mosque in Medina (tomorrow). Confirm the wording 'the early accounts say'.
Length of the stay at Quba varies in reports (e.g. four days in Ibn Ishaq, fourteen nights in a Bukhari report); the script says 'some days'.
'After thirteen years' in Mecca follows the common count; confirm.
